chromatographR: An introduction to HPLC-DAD analysis

Ethan Bass

2026-10-28

Source: vignettes/chromatographR.Rmd
chromatographR.Rmd

Introduction

chromatographR is a package for the reproducible analysis of HPLC-DAD data in R. Liquid chromatography coupled to diode-array detection (HPLC-DAD) remains one of the most popular analytical methodologies due to its convenience and low-cost. However, there are currently very few open-source tools available for analyzing HPLC-DAD chromatograms or other “simple” chromatographic data. chromatographR provides a scriptable, open-source alternative to proprietary GUI-based software, so an analysis can be exactly reproduced.

The chromatographR package began as a fork from the previously published alsace package (Wehrens et al. 2015), but has been reworked with improved functions for peak-finding, integration and peak table generation as well as a number of new tools for data visualization and downstream analysis. Unlike alsace, which emphasized multivariate curve resolution through alternating least squares (MCR-ALS), chromatographR is developed around a more conventional workflow that should seem more familiar to users of standard software tools for HPLC-DAD analysis. chromatographR includes tools for a) pre-processing, b) retention-time alignment, c) peak-finding, d) peak-integration and e) peak-table construction, as well as additional functions useful for analyzing the resulting peak table.

Workflow

Loading data

chromatographR can import data from a growing list of proprietary file formats using the read_chroms function from the chromConverter package. Supported file formats include ‘Agilent ChemStation’ and ‘MassHunter’ (.D) files, ‘Thermo Raw’ (.raw), ‘Chromeleon’ UV ASCII (.txt), ‘Waters ARW’ (.arw), ‘Shimadzu’ ASCII (.txt), and more. (For a complete list, see the chromConverter documentation). Select the appropriate file format by specifying the format_in argument (e.g., csv, chemstation_uv, masshunter_dad, chromeleon_uv, waters_arw, etc).

> path <- 'foo' # path to parent directory
> 
> # single folder
> read_chroms(paths = path, format_in = "chemstation_uv")
> 
> # multiple folders
> folders <- list.files(path = path, full.names = TRUE)
> dat <- read_chroms(folders, format_in = "chemstation_uv")

Example data

The package includes some example data consisting of root extracts from tall goldenrod (Solidago altissima). Roots were extracted in 90% methanol and run on an Agilent 1100 HPLC coupled to a DAD detector, according to a previously described method (Uesugi and Kessler 2013). The dataset is called Sa (abbreviated from Solidago altissima).

> data(Sa)

Pre-processing data

Data from liquid chromatography often carry non-informative artifacts, such as noise or a drifting baseline. The data may also have a higher resolution or wider range (along either the time or spectral dimensions) than we require. Smoothing reduces noise in the spectral direction, and baseline subtraction corrects a drifting baseline. Interpolating wavelengths and retention times reduces the dimensionality of the data, which makes samples easier to compare and cuts the time and memory that downstream analyses need. All three (smoothing, baseline correction, and interpolation) are available through the preprocess function and are enabled by default.

To select a narrower range of times and/or wavelengths, supply them to the optional dim1 and dim2 arguments.

Several estimators are available for baseline correction. Here we focus on the default estimator: asymmetric least squares ("als", via ptw::asysm (Bloemberg et al. 2010)), which fits a smooth curve to the signal while weighting points above the fit differently from points below it; the strength of that asymmetry is set by p and the stiffness of the curve by stiffness. Three other estimators are available – "arpls", "aspls" and "snip" – which differ in how they decide what counts as baseline (see ?baseline_estimators for further details).

The stiffness argument controls how rapidly the estimated baseline can vary. Larger values produce a stiffer baseline that follows only slower changes in the signal. The effective stiffness depends on the sampling interval, so the same value can produce different baselines for differently sampled data. Because baseline correction is applied after interpolation, the effective stiffness is determined by the dim1 grid. Accordingly, the time grid should be chosen before tuning stiffness.

> # choose dimensions for interpolation
> new_times <- seq(10, 18.66, by = .01) # choose time-points
> new_wavelengths <- seq(200, 318, by = 2) # choose wavelengths

Making the baseline too flexible is the failure mode to watch out for. Below, the zoomed chromatogram is plotted with two estimated baselines. At stiffness = 1e3 the baseline bends up into the peak shoulders around 12.5 and 13.8 minutes, and the signal it absorbs is subtracted from the peaks above it. At 2e5, the baseline follows the drift while remaining below the peak shoulders. There is no universally correct value here: what works depends mostly on how sharply your own baseline curves, which is why it is worth plotting the fit.

> i <- 2 # chromatogram number in list of data
> wavelength <- '200.00000' # this must match one of the column names from your chromatogram
> trace <- Sa[[i]][, wavelength, drop = FALSE]
> 
> fit_baseline <- function(stiffness){
+   preprocess(trace, dim1 = new_times, interpolate_cols = FALSE,
+              stiffness = stiffness, attach_baseline = TRUE,
+              show_progress = FALSE)
+ }
> too_flexible <- fit_baseline(1e3)
> about_right <- fit_baseline(2e5)
> 
> plot_baseline(too_flexible, lty=2, zoom = TRUE, annotate=FALSE, main="")
> plot_baseline(about_right, add=TRUE, col="darkgreen")
> legend("topright", c("stiffness = 1e3", "stiffness = 2e5"),
+        col = c("red", "darkgreen"), lty = c(2, 1), lwd = 2, bty = "n")

Estimated baselines on one wavelength of one chromatogram, plotted so that only the baseline region is visible (the peaks run off the top of the panel). At stiffness = 1e3 (red, dashed) the baseline rides up into the peak shoulders; at 2e5 (green) it follows only the drift.

The stiffness chosen above carries straight into the call below, which applies it to the whole dataset on the same time grid. For 2D data (e.g., from a single-wavelength detector), the dim2 argument should be left blank.

> dat.pr <- preprocess(Sa, dim1 = new_times, dim2 = new_wavelengths, 
+                      stiffness = 2e5, cl = 1)

Alignment

In many cases, liquid chromatography can suffer from retention time shifts of varying degree (e.g., due to temperature fluctuations, column degradation, or subtle changes in mobile-phase composition), which can make it very difficult to compare peaks across samples. Luckily, a number of “time-warping” algorithms have been developed for correcting these kinds of shifts. In chromatographR, the correct_rt function offers three: parametric time warping (ptw) (Eilers 2004; Bloemberg et al. 2010), variable penalty dynamic time warping (vpdtw) (Clifford et al. 2009; Clifford and Stone 2012), and landmark parametric time warping (lptw), which fits the warping polynomial to matched peak positions rather than to the full signal. The two covered below are ptw and vpdtw. Both warping functions aim to produce a better alignment of features by “warping” the time-axis of each supplied chromatogram to match a reference chromatogram. (The reference chromatogram can either be determined algorithmically or selected manually by setting the reference argument).

First, we check the alignment of our chromatograms using the plot_chroms function.

> plot_chroms(dat.pr, lambdas = 210, show_legend = TRUE)

Chromatographic traces of four S. altissima root chromatograms at 210 nm.

Our chromatograms appear to be shifted, as shown by the poor overlap of the chromatograms across our four samples. To remedy this problem, we can try to “warp” our chromatograms using one of the two options described above.

Parametric time warping

The ptw option can take a single wavelength or a list of wavelengths provided by the user using the lambdas argument. For each chromatogram, ptw then produces a “global” warping function across all the wavelengths supplied by the user. The code block below creates warping models for the samples in the provided list of data matrices. The same function is then used to warp each chromatogram according to the corresponding model, by setting the models parameter. Depending on the variety of your samples and the severity of the retention time shifts, it may take some experimentation with the warping parameters to get satisfactory results. Fewer peaks can work better here: a wavelength carrying fewer peaks sometimes yields a better warping model. (Also see the documentation for ptw for more guidance on warp function optimization).

> warping.models <- correct_rt(dat.pr, alg = "ptw", what = "models", lambdas = 210, scale = TRUE)
> warp_ptw <- correct_rt(chrom_list = dat.pr, models = warping.models, what = "corrected.values")

We can then use the following code snippet to compare the alignment of warped (top panel) and unwarped (bottom panel) chromatograms.

> par(mfrow=c(2,1))
> plot_chroms(dat.pr, lambdas = 210, show_legend = FALSE)
> legend("topleft", legend = "Raw data", bty = "n")
> 
> plot_chroms(warp_ptw, lambdas = 210, show_legend = FALSE)
> legend("topleft", legend = "PTW", bty = "n")

Comparison of parametric time warping (PTW) aligned chromatograms and raw data.

Clearly, the alignment is considerably improved after warping. You can also use the correct_rt function to do a global alignment on multiple wavelengths, by providing a list of wavelengths to the lambdas argument, but this will not always improve the results. While the alignment still isn’t perfect after warping, it is probably good enough to align our peaks and assemble them in the peak table, which is our primary goal.

Variable penalty dynamic time warping

Variable penalty dynamic time warping is another algorithm that can be very effective for correcting retention time shifts (Clifford et al. 2009; Clifford and Stone 2012). Instead of calculating an explicit warping function, dynamic time warping (DTW) works by repeatedly shifting, expanding or contracting the time axis in small steps until a satisfactory alignment is attained. This process can result in very close matching of peaks, but can also lead to severe peak distortion if the time axis is repeatedly expanded and/or contracted (Tomasi et al. 2004). Variable penalty dynamic time warping is a derivative of DTW that constrains expansion and contraction of the time-axis by applying a penalty to these types of “risky” moves. This often places peaks very closely, but it does not prevent distortion: a peak that falls where the warp changes is still stretched or squeezed, and its area changes with it (see Peak detection and integration below). Unlike PTW, VPdtw can only take a single wavelength as input (but it returns a global warping on the whole chromatographic matrix). The code snippet below uses VPdtw to warp the example chromatograms using the first chromatogram as a reference. The penalty, max_shift and dilation_span parameters can be adjusted to control the degree of warping. The latter two are widths along the time axis, given in minutes.

(Note: VPdtw is a suggested rather than a required dependency, since it needs a working C++ compiler.)

> vpdtw_models <- correct_rt(chrom_list = dat.pr, alg = "vpdtw", lambdas = 210,
+                            what = "models")
> warp_vpdtw <- correct_rt(chrom_list = dat.pr, models = vpdtw_models,
+                          alg = "vpdtw", lambdas = 210)
> par(mfrow=c(2,1))
> plot_chroms(dat.pr, lambdas = 210, show_legend = FALSE)
> legend("topleft", legend = "Raw data", bty = "n")
> 
> plot_chroms(warp_vpdtw, lambdas = 210, show_legend = FALSE)
> legend("topleft", legend = "VPdtw", bty = "n")

Comparison of variable penalty dynamic time warping (VPdtw) aligned chromatograms (top) with raw data (bottom).

Chromatograms can also be visualized as heatmaps with plot_chroms_heatmap, which can be a powerful way to check the alignment of chromatograms across samples.

> par(mfrow=c(3,1))
> plot_chroms_heatmap(dat.pr, lambdas = 210, show_legend = FALSE,
+                     title="Raw data")
> plot_chroms_heatmap(warp_ptw, lambdas = 210, show_legend = FALSE,
+                     title="Parametric Time Warping (PTW)")
> plot_chroms_heatmap(warp_vpdtw, lambdas = 210, show_legend = FALSE,
+                     title="Variable Penalty Dynamic Time Warping (VPdtw)")

Heatmaps of the raw chromatograms (top), and of the chromatograms aligned by parametric time warping (middle) and variable penalty dynamic time warping (bottom).

In this case the alignments produced by the two algorithms are quite similar, but in other cases one algorithm may dramatically outperform the other. PTW’s parametric warp can occasionally go awry and overwarp the data, distorting peaks. On the other hand, PTW fits an explicit model to each chromatogram, and its coefficients often reveal problematic samples.

Peak detection and integration

The get_peaks function produces a nested list of peaks by looping through the supplied chromatograms at the specified wavelengths, finding peaks, and fitting them to the specified function using non-linear least squares. The area under each fitted curve is then estimated by the trapezoidal rule. The fit argument specifies the peak model. By default, peaks are fit to an exponential-gaussian hybrid function ("egh") (Lan and Jorgenson 2001). The other models are the bidirectional exponentially modified gaussian ("bemg") and "gaussian". Alternatively, peak areas can be integrated without applying a model (fit = "raw"). The function returns a nested list of data.frames containing parameters for the peaks identified in each chromatogram.

Integrate the unaligned chromatograms (dat.pr), not the warped ones. Warping resamples the signal, so any peak it stretches or squeezes is no longer the peak that was measured, and its area is wrong. Alignment is still needed to decide which peaks are the same compound across samples; correct_peaks supplies it by mapping each peak’s retention time through the warping models, leaving areas untouched.

> # find and integrate peaks using bidirectional exponentially modified gaussian
> pks_bemg <- get_peaks(dat.pr, lambdas = c(210), fit = "bemg")
> 
> # find and integrate peaks using gaussian peak fitting
> pks_gauss <- get_peaks(dat.pr, lambdas = c(210), fit = "gaussian")
> 
> # find and integrate peaks using exponential-gaussian hybrid model
> pks_egh <- get_peaks(dat.pr, lambdas = c(210), fit = "egh")
> 
> # map retention times onto the aligned time axis
> pks_egh <- correct_peaks(pks_egh, mod_list = vpdtw_models, chrom_list = dat.pr)

Visualization

The plot.peak_list function shows how well the peaks were integrated. Below we compare the peaks fitted for the first chromatogram (idx = 1) using the three peak models. On these data, both asymmetric models fit more closely than the symmetric gaussian, as the r.squared column of each peak list shows.

> par(mfrow=c(3,1))
> plot(pks_gauss, idx = 1, lambda = 210)
> legend("topright", "Gaussian", bty = "n")
> 
> plot(pks_egh, idx = 1, lambda = 210)
> legend("topright", "Exponential-gaussian hybrid", bty = "n")
> 
> plot(pks_bemg, idx = 1, lambda = 210)
> legend("topright", "Bidirectional exponentially modified gaussian", bty = "n")

Comparison of peak models: gaussian (top), exponential-gaussian hybrid (middle) and bidirectional exponentially modified gaussian (bottom).

Local baseline correction

When peaks sit on a rising or falling background — for example, during gradient elution — the baseline argument fits a local baseline beneath each peak. Setting baseline = "flat" fits a constant offset per peak; baseline = "sloped" fits a linearly varying baseline across the peak window. In both cases peak heights and areas are computed above the fitted baseline.

The effect is most visible on data that has not been baseline-corrected during preprocessing. Below, we preprocess the raw data without baseline correction to better illustrate the difference.

> dat.pr.ubc <- preprocess(Sa[2], dim1 = new_times, dim2 = new_wavelengths,
+                         baseline = "none", cl = 1)
> 
> pks_ubc <- get_peaks(dat.pr.ubc, lambdas = 210, fit = "egh", cl = 1)
> pks_flat <- get_peaks(dat.pr.ubc, lambdas = 210, fit = "egh", baseline = "flat", cl = 1)
> pks_sloped <- get_peaks(dat.pr.ubc, lambdas = 210, fit = "egh", baseline = "sloped", cl = 1)
> 
> par(mfrow=c(3,1))
> plot(pks_ubc, lambda = 210)
> legend("topright", "Uncorrected", bty = "n")
> 
> plot(pks_flat, lambda = 210)
> legend("topright", "Flat baseline", bty = "n")
> 
> plot(pks_sloped, lambda = 210)
> legend("topright", "Sloped baseline", bty = "n")

Comparison of peak fitting with no baseline (top), a flat baseline (middle), and a sloped baseline (bottom) on un-baseline-corrected data. Shaded areas represent the fitted peak above the local baseline.

Peak filtering

The peak-finding algorithm often detects peaks that are little more than noise. Filtering these out at this stage reduces the cost of peak table construction, which matters most when there are many samples. Call filter_peaks on the peak_list to filter by peak width (min_fwhm, max_fwhm), height or area, or pass min_amplitude to get_peaks to drop low apices before they are fitted.

To set the width limits, and the peak-finding settings, from the widths of your own peaks, see the peak-finding article.

Peak table assembly

After obtaining a peak_list, the get_peaktable function links peaks across samples by hierarchical clustering (complete linkage on retention times, by default). It returns a peak_table object with samples as rows and peaks as columns. The peak_table object also has slots for holding metadata about peaks, samples, and the parameters used in the analysis. With many samples this step is expensive, so filter the peak_list before passing it to get_peaktable (see Peak filtering above). Peaks can also be filtered after peak_table assembly using the filter_peaktable function. An important parameter here is hmax, the height at which the clustering tree is cut, which controls how closely retention times must agree to be matched across samples. A low value of hmax increases the odds of splitting a single peak across multiple columns, while a high value increases the odds of combining multiple peaks into the same column.

Because pks_egh carries corrected retention times, get_peaktable clusters on those, and functions that later read spectra or traces from the peak table use the aligned chromatograms automatically, rebuilt from the warping models that correct_peaks stored.

> # assemble peak table from peak_list saved in `pks_egh`
> pk_tab <- get_peaktable(pks_egh, response = "area", hmax = 0.2)
> 
> # print first six columns of peak table
> head(pk_tab$tab[,1:6])
          V1       V2        V3        V4        V5        V6
119 0.000000 5.433084 0.6104369 2.0632364 15.065750 0.3051644
121 0.000000 4.183750 1.0255052 0.5964413  7.830246 0.0000000
122 3.814608 8.343632 0.6042582 2.0559778 25.787379 1.7809250
458 6.797762 6.311539 2.2515294 1.9966939 14.256253 1.2782027

If you only need a few known compounds, get_peaks(targets = ...) fits only the peaks at the retention times you list, and get_peaktable returns one named column per target. See ?targeted_analysis, and the targeted analysis article for a worked example.

Further analysis and data-visualization

Attaching metadata

To begin analyzing your peak table, you will usually want to attach sample metadata to the peak_table object. Use the attach_metadata function. Its metadata argument takes a data.frame of experimental metadata with one column matching your sample names; name that column as a string in the column argument. The ordered metadata is stored in the sample_meta slot of your peak table. The peak table can then be normalized (e.g., by dividing out the sample weight) using the normalize_data function.

> # load example metadata
> path <- system.file("extdata", "Sa_metadata.csv", package = "chromatographR")
> meta <- read.csv(path)
> # attach metadata
> pk_tab <- attach_metadata(peak_table = pk_tab, metadata = meta, column = "vial")
> # normalize peak table by sample mass
> pk_tab <- normalize_data(peak_table = pk_tab, column = "mass")

Attaching reference spectra

Optionally, attach scaled reference spectra to the peak_table with the attach_ref_spectra function. This can be helpful for working with UV spectra programmatically (e.g., to sort peaks by their chromophores). Reference spectra are defined either as the spectrum with the highest intensity for each peak (when ref = "max.int") or as the spectrum with the highest average correlation to the other spectra associated with the peak (when ref = "max.cor"). Below we use these spectra to construct a correlation matrix and find peaks matching a particular chromophore.

> pk_tab <- attach_ref_spectra(pk_tab, ref = "max.int")
> cor_matrix <- cor(pk_tab$ref_spectra)
> hx <- names(which(cor_matrix[,"V21"] > .97))
> matplot(x = as.numeric(rownames(pk_tab$ref_spectra)),
+                    y = pk_tab$ref_spectra[, hx], type = 'l',
+                    ylab = "Abs (mAU)", 
+                    xlab = "Wavelength (nm)")

Data visualization

Mirror plot

The mirror_plot function provides a quick way to visually compare results across treatment groups.

> mirror_plot(pk_tab, lambdas = c(210), var = "trt", legend_size = 2)

Plotting spectra

The plot_spectrum function plots or returns the spectra associated with a particular peak in your peak table – useful for checking whether the spectra for a peak match across samples, or for comparing one against a known standard. Set plot_spectrum or plot_trace to FALSE to draw only the other. By default it plots the trace and spectrum from the chromatogram with the largest peak in the peak table; idx and lambda choose the chromatogram and wavelength instead.

> par(mfrow = c(2,1))
> peak <- "V8"
> plot_spectrum(peak, peak_table = pk_tab, chrom_list = warp_vpdtw,
+               verbose = FALSE)

The plot_spectrum function also generates interactive plots using plotly.

> plot_spectrum(peak, peak_table = pk_tab, chrom_list = warp_vpdtw, 
+               verbose = FALSE, engine = "plotly")

The plot_all_spectra function compares the spectra for a specified peak across all samples.

> par(mfrow=c(1,2))
> plot_all_spectra("V14", peak_table = pk_tab, export_spectrum = FALSE)
> plot_all_spectra("V15", peak_table = pk_tab, export_spectrum = FALSE)

Inconsistent spectra, as in V14, can indicate a problem with the alignment, or co-elution of several substances in the same retention window. By contrast, V15 looks relatively pure.

The plot_spectrum_inset function plots spectra onto the chromatogram.

> plot_spectrum_inset("V14", peak_table = pk_tab, 
+               verbose = FALSE, xlab="Retention time (min)",
+               position="top", inset_width = 0.25)

Passing several peaks draws one inset per peak, titled by the names of loc. Additional peaks can be labeled with arbitrary labels using the annotate_peaks function.

> plot_spectrum_inset(c("Unknown 1" = "V8",
+                       "Unknown 2" = "V16"), idx=c(1:4), 
+                     peak_table = pk_tab, 
+               verbose = FALSE, xlab="Retention time (min)",
+               position=list(c(0.0,0.6),c(0.55,0.4)), inset_width = 0.25,
+               scale_spectrum = FALSE) |>
+    annotate_peaks(loc = c(A = "V6", B = "V8", C="V18",
+                           D = "V22", E = "V23"), peak_table = pk_tab)

Plot peak table function

The plot.peak_table function is a simplified interface to the plots above: it dispatches to plot_spectrum and plot_all_spectra, and compares results across treatments by calling boxplot.

> par(mfrow = c(3,1))
> plot(pk_tab, loc = "V14", box_plot = TRUE, vars = "trt", verbose = FALSE)
